source.title: Improving Sparse Autoencoder with Dynamic Attention
source.authors: Dong-Sheng Wang; Jinsen Zhang; Da-Wei Su; Hui Huang

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains and evaluates sparse autoencoders on GPT-2 Small activations, reporting reconstruction results relevant to whether an SAE dictionary can recover features; it does not use the original toy-model geometry experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper cites superposition as motivation but does not test toy networks, feature-overlap geometry, or neuron-level polysemanticity. Its GPT-2 experiments report SAE reconstruction, not direct tests of semantic feature recovery or feature geometry. The additional ImageNet/CLIP sparsity, interpretability, failure-case, and zero-shot classification results are visual-model results and do not test the LLM-specific V4 claim; the sparsity and interpretability metrics and explicit failure cases are recorded as findings outside the listed versions. Zero-shot classification tables 7–17 report many visual-model outcomes, which are not separately catalogued because they do not bear on a listed version.
record.test_reason: A new SAE architecture paper. Superposition is cited only as motivation. Every result compares the authors' Sparsemax SAE with other SAEs: NMSE and CE on GPT-2 Small; zero-shot accuracy, sparsity and interpretability on CLIP. No result asks whether GPT-2 holds sparse recoverable features, how features are spread across neurons, or how features are laid out geometrically. It relies on the finding as a tool and reports its own method's performance, so it is T4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that a cross-attention SAE with sparsemax picks the number of active concepts per sample, improving reconstruction and concept quality over ReLU/TopK SAEs. Text evidence is reconstruction only (NMSE and CE on GPT-2); concept-quality evidence is visual only (CLIP). They also claim the sparsemax-inferred K (24) helps tune TopK SAEs.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and evaluates a sparsemax-attention SAE, not the original toy-network feature-vector and interference experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The text reconstruction results vary with dataset and dictionary size; the study does not report a controlled sweep of feature sparsity or feature importance.

fits_no_version.finding: On GPT-2 Small layer 8, the Sparsemax SAE reports lower NMSE than ReLU, JumpReLU, Gated, TopK and BatchTopK SAEs at all four dictionary sizes on both corpora.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparsemax-attention SAEs reconstruct LLM activations with lower NMSE than standard SAE variants (method comparison).

fits_no_version.finding: On CLIP ViT-B/16, the paper reports sparsity, reconstruction and monosemanticity metrics for the Sparsemax SAE vs ReLU, TopK and BatchTopK SAEs. It also notes qualitative failure cases (unclear concepts, possible feature absorption, near-duplicate concepts).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision SAEs of different architectures trade off sparsity, reconstruction and monosemanticity scores; even the best show absorbed or near-duplicate concepts.

record.peer_reviewed: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (venue stated in metadata)
record.problems: The GPT-2 evaluation reports reconstruction metrics but does not directly assess semantic quality, stability, or dimensional geometry of recovered language-model features. The paper reports explicit visual concept failure cases. Numerical uncertainty estimates are not reported for the tabled results.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. The detailed visual zero-shot classification results in Figure 3 and Tables 7–17 are not catalogued as they concern CLIP image classification rather than a listed LLM claim.

untested.parts: All parts: no toy models, no sparsity transition, no geometry.
All parts: no capacity or importance analysis.
All parts: no tests of polysemanticity's causes.
Whether GPT-2 features are distributed across neurons or recoverable as sparse features. Only SAE-vs-SAE reconstruction comparisons are reported.
Completeness, stability and canonicality of SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' label is removed. The study is a method-comparison (T4) paper, and better reconstruction by one SAE variant over others does not bear on whether LLMs contain sparse recoverable features. The authors say Sparsemax shows 'reduced CE degradation' across all settings, but Table 2 has TopK/BatchTopK at higher values on OpenWeb M=3072 and M=12288. The CE sign convention is never explained.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, more sparse features than dimensions, overlap and near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether feature importance or limited capacity causes dedicated dimensions versus feature sharing.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity and whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.

The GPT-2 experiments measure reconstruction, not semantic quality or stability of recovered language-model features, nor whether features are distributed across neurons. CLIP visual-model metrics do not test the LLM-specific claim.
Completeness, stability, and canonical status of SAE features.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional subspaces.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GPT2 Small; OpenWeb and WikiText-103 reconstruction tests at dictionary sizes M = 3072, 6144, 12288, and 24576
reader_labels.reason: Sparsemax SAE produces reported reconstruction results on GPT-2 activations across both datasets and all tested dictionary sizes (R1–R16); this supports SAE-based recovery at the reconstruction level, not semantic feature validation.
